title: What It Means to Shepherd the Flock
subtitle: On the shepherd image, the daily demands of pastoral care, and why feeding, leading, and guarding the flock of God still defines the work

sections.title: A Word With Mud On It
sections.body:
The Bible did not reach for a clean word. It reached for a shepherd. A man who smelled like the animals he kept, who slept in the open, who walked behind a flock too stupid to find water on its own and too frightened to cross a stream without him.

We have softened the word until it means almost nothing. We put it on coffee mugs.

But a shepherd in the ancient world was not a sentimental figure. He was a worker with cracked hands who lost sleep and lost weight and sometimes lost blood for animals that could not say thank you. David killed a lion and a bear before he killed a giant, and he killed them over sheep. That is the word God chose for the men he sets over his people. Not executive. Not visionary. Not brand. Shepherd. I have wanted the cleaner words. I have wanted the office with my name on the door more than the field with mud on my boots. The word does not let me. The word keeps dragging me back to the animals.

sections.title: Feed the Flock
sections.body:
A shepherd who does not feed the sheep is not a shepherd. He is a man who owns sheep and lets them starve. The first command Jesus gave Peter by the fire was not lead, not grow, not build. It was feed my lambs.

Feeding is the slow work. It is the study no one sees and the sermon they forget by Tuesday.

The flock eats every week, which means you cook every week, which means there is no season when you have arrived. Ezekiel stood over the false shepherds of Israel and his charge against them was specific. You eat the fat. You clothe yourselves with the wool. You do not feed the sheep. The temptation of the pastorate is to feed yourself on the flock instead of feeding the flock from the Word. To use the people for your platform. To let your hunger for significance eat the very animals you were given to nourish. I know that hunger. I have caught myself preparing a sermon to be admired instead of a meal to be eaten. The flock can tell the difference. They go home hungry and they cannot always say why.

sections.title: Lead From the Front
sections.body:
Eastern shepherds did not drive their sheep. They walked in front of them, and the sheep followed because they knew the voice. This is the whole pattern of pastoral leadership and we have inverted it. We drive from behind with programs and pressure and guilt.

The sheep follow a voice they trust. They do not follow a strategy they were sold.

Leading from the front means the pastor goes first into the things he asks of others. First into confession. First into generosity. First into the hard conversation and the costly forgiveness. You cannot lead a flock into a place you are unwilling to walk yourself. Peter, writing to elders, says it plainly. Not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock. Example, not pressure. The man who lords it over the sheep has forgotten that the sheep are not his. They are the flock of God, bought with blood that was not the shepherd's own. I have led by pressure when I was too tired to lead by example. It worked for a season and it cost me trust I did not get back cheaply.

sections.title: Guard the Flock
sections.body:
There are wolves. The New Testament says so without apology, and it says they will come from inside the church wearing the wool of the very sheep they intend to eat. A shepherd who will not name a wolf is not gentle. He is asleep.

Guarding is the unpopular half of love. It makes enemies. It is love anyway.

Paul wept over the Ephesian elders and warned them that savage wolves would come in among them, and that from their own number men would arise speaking twisted things to draw away disciples. The job is not only to feed the sheep but to stand between the sheep and what would devour them. False teaching. Predatory men. The slow poison of a divisive person who has decided the church belongs to him. Guarding costs you the reputation of being nice. It will earn you the accusation that you are unloving, when in fact the unloving thing would be to let the wolf eat. I have stayed quiet when I should have stood in the gate, because standing in the gate is lonely and the wolf had friends. The sheep paid for my silence. They always do.

sections.title: The Shepherd Over the Shepherds
sections.body:
Here is the mercy buried in the demand. You are not the owner. You are an under-shepherd, and there is a Chief Shepherd who will appear, and the flock was always his.

That changes everything about the weight. The weight is real, but it is not finally yours.

You will not save these people. You cannot. You can feed and lead and guard, and then you must hand them back every night to the one who laid down his life for them when you could only lay down an evening. The Good Shepherd did not lose one the Father gave him. Your job is faithfulness, not omnipotence, and the difference between those two words is the difference between a pastor who lasts and a pastor who burns to the ground trying to be God for people who already have one. When the Chief Shepherd appears, Peter says, you will receive the unfading crown of glory. Not for building the largest flock. For tending the one you were given. So tend it. Feed, lead, guard, and then go to sleep, because the sheep belong to him and he does not sleep.
